name: Boxed protocol type
first: A type that can hold a value of any type that conforms to a protocol, whose real type is found only while the program runs. It is also called an existential type.

dependsOn.why: A boxed protocol type is written with a protocol's name, and holds values of the types that conform to it.
dependsOn.whyInExample: `any Shape` holds values of `Square` and `Strip`, the two types that conform to `Shape`.

dependsOn.why: A boxed protocol type is the other way to hide a value's type, and differs from an opaque type, which holds one real type.

what.is: A boxed protocol type is written as `any` followed by a protocol's name. A value of this type can be a value of any type that conforms to the protocol, and its real type is found only while the program runs. Swift's documentation also calls it an existential type.
what.afterExample: The array `tiles` holds a `Square` and a `Strip`, two different types, because the type of its elements is `any Shape`.
what.problem: Code sometimes keeps values of different types together, such as the tiles of a floor, some square and some long. An array's elements all have one type. With `any Shape` as that type, each element can be a value of any type that conforms to `Shape`.
what.how: Each value of type `any Shape` is kept together with its real type. When code calls `area()` on it, the program finds the real type while it runs, and calls the `area()` of that type.

when.text: Use one when a value's type can differ from value to value, or change over time, such as the elements of `tiles`.
Don't use one when every value has the same real type. An opaque type, written with the keyword some, keeps that one type, so swiftc knows it.

parts.name: The keyword `any`, line 16
parts.text: The keyword `any` before `Shape` makes `any Shape` a boxed protocol type. The array's type, `[any Shape]`, lets each element be a value of a different type that conforms to `Shape`.

steps.text: Lines 16 to 19 make an array of two elements, a `Square` whose `side` is 3 and a `Strip` whose `length` is 5, and store it in `tiles`. Each element keeps its real type.
The loop on line 20 takes the first element. Line 21 prints its real type, `Square`, and calls `area()`, which runs the `area()` of `Square` on line 7: {{Square 9}}.
The loop takes the second element. This time `area()` runs the `area()` of `Strip` on line 13, and line 21 prints {{Strip 5}}.

end.text: Each element of `[any Shape]` keeps its own real type, and the call of `area()` on line 21 runs the method of that type.
